listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to Miami. A few things before the doors open. If you have not checked in yet, the registration desk is at the Hall A entrance, and it closes at eight thirty. Please have your QR code ready. It is in your confirmation email and in the conference app. The app is also the fastest way to get your bearings. It has the floor plan, the full agenda and the four tracks: payments, digital assets, regulation and small business. Shuttles to the partner hotels leave every twenty minutes from the south entrance, and the last one tonight is at eleven. The networking lounge on the second floor is open all day, with coffee and quiet tables for meetings. And one last reminder. The side events this evening are by invitation only, so please check the app for your invitations before six. Have a great first day.

Oh, this is my third time here, so I know the feeling. The first year, I spent the whole morning walking in circles. Now I do it differently. I've been here since seven, and I've been sitting in the networking lounge most of the time, because that is where people actually stop and talk. My advice? Do not make the rounds of the booths before lunch. In the morning everybody is fresh and busy, and the vendors are only interested in the big names. After lunch, they have been standing for five hours, and they are happy to talk to anybody. And go to the side events in the evening. That is where the real conversations start.

Sorry, I've got about two minutes. I've been running between sessions all morning. I'm on the regulation track. I work in compliance, for a bank in Charlotte. Latin America? Yes, actually, that's interesting. We've been looking at Brazil for about a year, mostly because of instant payments. Our problem is not the technology. It's knowing who is on the other side of the payment. Look, I have to go, my panel starts at eleven. Here's my card. Send me an email today, not next week. And put the word Brazil in the subject line, otherwise it gets lost with the other two hundred emails from this conference.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a series of sessions on the same topic that runs through the whole conference
to understand where you are and how a new place is organized
a smaller meeting, breakfast or reception organized around a conference, often by invitation
to start feeling confident in a new situation after a slow beginning
a quiet area with sofas and coffee where attendees sit down and meet people
to arrive at an event or a hotel and register, usually to collect a badge or a key
the phone application with the agenda, the floor plan and the list of attendees
a bus that takes people between the hotels and the conference center on a fixed schedule

paras: Arriving at a conference you have never attended is a strange experience, even for somebody who has been going to industry events for twenty years. At the events you know, you know the layout, the people and the rhythm. At a new event, you know nobody, the signs seem to be in the wrong places, and everybody else seems to have been there before. The first ninety minutes decide how the rest of the day goes, and most people waste them.

The first job is to get your bearings. Check in early, before the queue at the registration desk grows, and spend ten minutes with the conference app: the floor plan, the list of speakers and the tracks. Choose one track and ignore the others. People who try to follow everything usually end the day having seen nothing properly.

The second job is to talk to somebody within the first half hour. Not the most important person in the room, just somebody. The coffee station, the queue for the shuttle and the networking lounge are the easiest places, because nobody is in a hurry there. The opener does not need to be clever. I just got in this morning, so I'm still finding my footing is honest, and it invites the other person to help. Have you been to this one before? works for the same reason: people enjoy being the expert.

Only then should you start to make the rounds of the booths. Experienced attendees rarely work the room in the first hour. They wait until they have found their footing, and they keep their best energy for the afternoon, when the side events begin and the real conversations happen over a drink.

One more thing, about speed. A speaker who is nervous talks faster, and a listener who is nervous hears everything as faster. So slow your first sentence down on purpose, by about fifteen percent. To the other person, slow does not sound hesitant. It sounds like somebody who has been doing this for years.

To argue that your first conversation should always be with the most important person in the room.
